en: This implements the model of Granovetter (1978), "Threshold Models of Collective Behavior", American Journal of Sociology 83(6). The classic example (thresholds 0, 1, 2, …, 99) and the case with one person changed reproduce the paper's famous illustration with 100 people; verify with node tools/validate-revolution.js.

The normal-distribution thresholds (mean 20%, spread 15%, 1% instigators) are this project's settings, not the paper's numbers. Across 20 runs of the default settings every run reached 100%, and with 0% instigators every run stayed at 0%. At a mean of 25% the outcomes split anywhere from 2% to 100%.

Graph ④ keeps the current spread and instigator share, changes only the mean threshold, and runs 6 times each. With a classic example, ①–③ show 100 people with thresholds exactly 0, 1%, 2%, …, while ④ stays based on the normal distribution.
The code is available on GitHub.
Rumor Spread in Group Chats · Simulatio Lab
How fast does a rumor spread in group chats, and how late can a correction come and still matter? Try it yourself.
A single rumor posted in a group chat becomes common knowledge within hours. By what routes does a rumor spread, and how late can a correction come and still matter?
People belong to several group chats (dots are people, squares are chat rooms), and rooms differ in size, so there are big and small ones.
People who know the rumor post it in every room they belong to. Someone who sees it for the first time in a room is tempted with some probability and reposts it in their own rooms next round.
Each time they post, they lose interest and stop with some probability.

From the chosen moment, a correction starts to spread. We assume the correction is less tempting than the rumor (70% as much), and anyone who sees the correction neither believes nor spreads the rumor.

③ The Threshold of Temptation
The horizontal axis is the chance of being tempted, the vertical axis is the share of people who eventually learn the rumor. Each dot is one run.
④ Late Corrections Don't Help
The horizontal axis is when the correction starts, the vertical axis is the share of people the rumor reached. The dashed line is the case with no correction at all.

What it shows: Once the "chance of being tempted" crosses a threshold, the rumor suddenly reaches almost everyone. A correction works better the earlier it comes and barely helps once the rumor has spread widely. People in several rooms act as bridges between rooms.

What it doesn't show: It doesn't mean rumors in real group chats spread by these numbers. The content of the rumor, trust in the sender and the mood of the room are not captured, and the assumption that a correction is 70% as tempting as a rumor is only an assumption.

We placed an SIR-type rumor model (unaware → spreading → stopped) on a network of people and chat rooms, and added the correction as a second spreading process. It does not reproduce a specific paper; it is this project's own design.

500 people and 50 rooms; room popularity is proportional to rank^−0.6 so that big and small rooms appear. A person who spreads the rumor posts in every room they belong to, and the chance of losing interest is 70%.
Graphs ③ and ④ change only the given value in the current setup and run it several times.

Why Birds of a Feather Flock Together · Simulatio Lab
Can a mild wish not to be a minority split a neighborhood completely apart? Run the Schelling segregation model yourself.
"I don't mind a diverse neighborhood. I just want a third of my neighbors to be like me." Could a neighborhood of such tolerant people still split almost completely apart?
On a grid, two groups, blue and orange, live randomly mixed, and some cells are empty.
Everyone is content if at least a certain share of their 8 surrounding neighbors belong to their own group. That share is the slider's "desired share."
An unhappy person moves to a random empty cell. This repeats until everyone is happy.
Nobody says "I don't want to live with the other group." They only say "I don't want to be a minority."
